4.5 How to set up the data set so the analysis is much easier to perform
Let’s set this up to work with virtually ANY data set, not just Boston Housing. We’ll do that in two steps:

Rename the target column as ‘y’
Always move the target column to the right most position

These two steps will make it much easier to do our analysis using different modeling methods.






The big secret at this point is to format all the data sets in the same layout. Not just the Boston Housing data set, but the other data sets we will use, too. The last column will always be the target column, and always named ‘y’.   ggplot2::labs(title = 'Bagging predicted vs actual', x = 'Actual', y = 'Predicted')

Welcome to Hands On Ensemble Methods With R! I hope you find this to be a very rewarding book. This has been a pure delight and joy to work on and create, and I hope that sense is communicated to you!






The purpose of this chapter is to give you an overview of the book, so you are well prepared to get the most from the contents.



The book is in two sections: Building ensembles of models (chapters 1 - 8), and working in the industry (chapters 9 - 15).

Part 1: Building ensembles of models

This section of the book is designed to give you tools to build ensembles of models that will be:

Easy to build, tailor, and optimize via tuning or cross-validation.
Usable with a very wide variety of data sets (so you do not need to keep building new models over and over for the same type of data).
Run very fast
Run with minimal (or zero) errors or warnings
Various levels of reproducible results.
Include graphs, charts and tables to help your reader understand the truth in the data.
You will be able to add many professional options in your model building, such as:

Multiple ways to automatically handle strings
Multiple ways to automatically resolve issues with highly correlated data
Ways to automatically complete stratified sampling of data
Multiple data reduction methods
Determine the most accurate model, and the strongest predictors for any given data set








You will be building ensembles of models of numeric, classification, logistic, time series, and survival data sets as you work through the book. You may use your results on your resume, portfolio, job interview, conference presentation, professional publication or anywhere you would like.




Examples of the results that you will achieve in this book using ensembles

Numeric ensembles:
• You will build ensembles of models that will have a lower root mean squared error (RMSE) than 20 years of the best scores in Kaggle data science competitions for the Boston Housing data set.
• You will build ensembles of models that will beat the best scores measuring the strength of concrete data set.
• Determine which features in the data separate the highest five percent of results from the lowest five percent of results.
• Summary results will include highest accuracy and strongest predictor.
Classification ensembles:
• 100% accuracy predicting heart disease using only the data - no medical test is required.
• 100% accuracy predicting maternal health risk from the data alone.
Logistic ensembles
• Sports analytics—You will model the on-court performance of professional athletes (such as Lebron James) and make evidence based recommendations for them to improve their performance
• Talent analytics—You will model employees and make evidence based recommendations to improve job satisfaction.
Forecasting ensembles
• You will make forecasts about the labor market in the United States, by combining data from the United States Department of Labor, and external data sources
• You will make forecasts about the winning times in marathons
Survival ensembles
(need to finish this section on survival ensembles)
We will be looking at making predictions in a very wide range of data, from sports to insurance, placing items on the shelf (retail analytics), diagnosing various diseases (heart disease, cancer, etc.), risk, talent analytics, public (government) analytics, and much more. All of these results (and more!) can be used in demonstrations, on your resume or portfolio, or any other place you would like to show your work.

“Test everything, hold on to the good.” St.Paul, 1st century

One of the important ways we will improve our models is by testing them over and over. We will build teams of rival models, with the goal of having a result that is superior to any individual or other ensemble of models.
We will randomly resample our models to see how the data changes when it is resampled. We will look at multiple ways of checking the accuracy of our models, to test if we have the optimal result.

More than the act of testing, the act of designing tests is one of the best bug preventers known. The thinking that must be done to create a useful test can discover and eliminate bugs before they are coded - indeed, test-design thinking can discover and eliminate bugs at every stage in the creation of software, from conception to specification, to design, coding and the rest.

Boris Bezier, quoted in Software Testing Techniques, Creating a Software Engineering Culture by Karl Eugene Wiegers

We will learn to design tests that return the most accurate description of the results. You will see multiple ways to test everything, and be better equipped to know which test is superior (or inferior), and why this is the case.

Why reverse engineering can speed up your code writing much faster than any AI system

I was getting ready to speak at a conference, and was being asked what I would be presenting. I explained that it is a system that allows people in data science to code extremely fast. “Faster than vibe coding?” one person asked. “Absolutely,” I replied. “Faster than coding assistants?” another asked. “Yes, faster than coding assistants.
I demonstrated how reverse engineering solved coding issues in seconds (literally) that vibe coding and AI assistance cannot match. The goal of clear and simple coding fits this quote:

The best programs are written so that computing machines can perform them quickly and so that human beings can understand them clearly. Donald E. Knuth

We will also look at ways to debug code that actually solves the real problem in the code.

The trick is to fix the problem you have, not the problem you want. Bram Cohen

Spend at least twice as much time seeking to understand the customer problem than solving it.

Part 2: Working in the industry







The second part of the book will improve your data science skills by improving your skills at finding customer issues, solving the true customer issues, communicating clearly, and delivering results the customer needs.



I’ve worked for over 30 years as a professional recruiter, and hired over 15,000 people. Here are some of the very interesting points I’ve learned along the way about what employers are looking for in the candidates they select, which we will discuss in this book:
• Employers want results and accomplishments, and are willing to pay for it! We will look at many examples where we will seek to understand the needs of the company, and how we can deliver data science results that meet or exceed the needs of the customer.
• Employers want employees who can solve real problems for their customers. We will look at how data science can help you build solutions for your customers in ways that solve real problems for their customers. We will see ways we can test this hypothesis, and fix our methods when we do not meet the expectations.
• Soft skills can put you far ahead of the competition. Once we have built our models, we will look at ways to present the results that greatly increase the chance of the solutions being accepted. We will test the accuracy of listening, problem understanding, and feasibility, as major ways to get your data science solution implemented.
• Employers want employees who can deliver models that are accurate, fast, and fully reproducible. In this book you will build ensembles of models that will be previous best results in Kaggle competitions. The models will run in a very short amount of time, and be fully reproducible.
• We will cover several advanced skills in the second half of the book. These will include how to predict on totally new data, hiring and getting hired, a code of ethics, contributing to the profession, and moving from student to professional to leader.
The combination of very strong data science skills, great skills understanding the customer, and the ability to communicate this at a very clear level is designed to give you the ultimate competitive advantage in the marketplace: A person who delivers fully reproducible and error free results the customer needs, in a way that is very professional, and maintains the highest standards of ethics and integrity.

How to test the accuracy of your understanding of the customer’s issues/problems/opportunities.

We will take an in-depth look at testing the understanding of the customer’s issues, and how to have the most accurate understanding of the customer issues. We will look at several real examples there the root issue is a misunderstanding of the customer, which led to unintended problems and consequences with the customer. These problems could have been avoided by testing the understanding of the customer’s issues before beginning the analysis.






Optimize financial performance, not staff productivity.



The report from MIT, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business in 2025 has a very stark warning about not understanding the customer’s needs:

Despite $30–40 billion in enterprise investment into GenAI, this report uncovers a surprising result in that 95% of organizations are getting zero return. The outcomes are so starkly divided across both buyers (enterprises, mid-market, SMBs) and builders (startups, vendors, consultancies) that we call it the GenAI Divide. Just 5% of integrated AI pilots are extracting millions in value, while the vast majority remain stuck with no measurable P&L impact. This divide does not seem to be driven by model quality or regulation, but seems to be determined by approach.

Misunderstanding the customer’s needs can possibly create more problems than bad code can ever cause. You can do a world of good making sure you truly understand the customer’s needs BEFORE you begin coding!
Early in my career I had the wonderful opportunity to receive very special customer service training, and I’ve remembered it all these years. The customer service training was using the Ritz-Carlton methods, and I found it truly amazing.
As it was explained to us, the world’s best customer service does not start with the customer—it always starts with the staff. We were trained to understand the true needs of the customer before we started to solve customer issues.

Companies will pay good money for people who can actually solve real customer problems.

In my decades in business I found it very useful to test my understanding of the customer’s true problem:
“If we provide this (list our current understanding of the customer’s problems and requests), will that meet all your requirements?”
“No, you’ve missed two key points.”
“Thank you for letting us know about the two key points we missed. We want to get those resolved for you.”
The more accurately you understand the customer’s needs, the less time you’ll need to spend fixing mistakes due to misunderstandings. The payoff for understanding customer needs up front is much larger than it seems at first.

Quick wrap-up

The book has two sections: Building models and working in the industry. The goal for both sections is to provide the best skills in modeling and working in the industry.

3.1 How a Chicago blizzard led to the very unlikely story of the best solutions to supervised data
My journey to the most advanced AI in the world started with an actual blizzard in Chicago. It might seem like Chicago would never get a blizzard, but we did in 2011, and it was incredibly intense, as this video shows:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cPiFn52ztd8
What does the Chicago 2011 Snomageddon have to do with the creation of the most advanced AI? Everything. Here’s the story.
At the time of the 2011 Blizzard I worked a Recruiter for Kelly Services, where I had worked since 1996. I agreed to work out of the Kelly Services office in Frankfort, Illinois at this time, though I worked out of nearly every Kelly Services office in the greater Chicago area at one time or another. The trip to Frankfort involved a daily commute to the office, but I was able to make the best use of the time on the road.
My manager at the time let me know several days in advance that there was a very large amount of snow forecast, and that I might want to be prepared. The most recent forecasts for large amounts of snow in the Chicago area all amounted to nothing. The weather was perfectly normal days in the Chicago area without any snow, so I predicted this storm would also be nothing, based on the most recent results. This was a great example of a prior prediction not transferring well to a current situation.
That morning I went to work as normal, and did not even look at the weather forecast. Around 2:45 pm my manager came out of her office and said “Russ, you need to come here and look at the weather radar!”. I walked into her office, and saw a map of a winter storm that was incredibly huge, one of the largest storms I ever saw. She had the image zoomed out, so it was possible to see several states, all covered by this gigantic storm. From what I could tell, the massive snow storm was barreling down on Chicago, and was about 15 minutes away from my location.
I told the candidate I was interviewing that I was leaving immediately, and that he is not allowed to stay. He has to get home as fast as possible for his own safety.
The storm started dropping snow on my trip north back home. The commute took around 50% longer than normal due to the rapidly falling snow.
As I later learned, the storm was forecast to start in the Chicago area around 3:00 pm, finish up between 11:00 am - 1:00 pm two days later, and leave 17 - 19 inches of snow.
How bad was it? Even City of Chicago snow plows were stopped by the snow
To see what the forecasts looked like, check out this news report from the day:
https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/blizzard-unleashes-winter-fury/2096753/
It turns out all three predictions of the blizzard were accurate to a level that seemed uncanny to me, and I had never noticed before: Start time, accumulation, and end time were all accurate. This is the first time I recall ever seeing a prediction at this level of accuracy. I had no idea this type of predictive accuracy was even possible. This level of accuracy in predicting results totally blew me away. I had never seen anything with this level of accuracy, and now I wanted to know how it was done.
I searched and searched for how the accuracy was so high for this forecast, but found nothing.
The power of the method—whatever it was—was obvious to me. I realized that if it could work for the weather, the solution method could work in an incredibly broad range of situations. A few of many other areas include business forecasts, production work, modeling prices, and much, much more. But that this point I had no idea how the accurate prediction was done.
Some months later a person wrote to Tom Skilling, chief meteorologist for WGN TV in Chicago, asking how the forecasts were so accurate. Tom posted an answer that opened up the solution for me. Here is the relevant part of Tom Skilling’s answer to a 2011 storm how the forecast was so accurate:
So that was the first step. Ensembles were the way they achieved such extraordinary prediction accuracy.
My next goal was to figure out how ensembles were made. As I looked up information, it became obvious that ensembles had been used for a while, such as the winning entry in the Netflix Prize Competition.
The Netflix Prize Competition was sponsored by Netflix to create a method to accurately predict user ratings on films. The minimum winning score needed to beat the Netflix method (named Cinematch) by at least 10%. Several years of work went into solving this problem, and the results even included several published papers. The winning solution was an ensemble of methods that beat the Cinematch results by 10.09%.
So it was now clear to me that ensembles were the path forward. However, I had no idea how to make ensembles.
I went to graduate school to study data science and predictive analytics. My degree was completed in 2017, from Northwestern University. However, I still was not sure how ensembles of models were built, nor could I find any clear methods to build them (except for pre-made methods, such as random forests). While it is true there were packages that could do some of the work, nothing I found did what I was looking for: How to build ensembles of models in general. Despite playing with the idea and looking online, I was not able to build the ensembles I wanted to build.

3.3 What most strongly predicts accurate results for predictions and forecasts?
Philip Tetlock conducted research to determine if the forecasts of some people can be consistently more accurate than the general public or experts. He was able to find such people, and identified them as Superforecasters. In summary, Superforecasters are not necessarily smarter than others. What strongly predicts their accuracy is a set of skills the use when predicting and forecasting. Using these skills provides greater accuracy than the general public or experts.
The Ensembles package, and the skills we will learn in this book, apply these skills to the problem of finding the best models for data. According to Tetlock, some of those traits include (page 191):
• Cautious in thinking — Nothing is certain
• Humble — Reality is infinitely complex
• Nondeterministic — What happens is not meant to be and does not have to happen
• Actively Open-Minded — Beliefs are hypotheses to be tested, not treasures to be protected
• Probabilistic: Judge using many grades of maybe
• Thoughtful updaters — When facts change, they change their minds
There are more traits, and I highly recommend the Superforecasting book to get a more accurate understanding of the best skills in prediction and forecasting.
As we will see in this book, we will combine diverse individual and ensembles of models, then repeat the process over and over again, to give the most accurate predictions and forecasts from the data.
We will actively seek disconfirmation of our models by two different methods. One is testing our models against a neutral data set, the other is testing against totally unseen data. We will measure the accuracy of both methods, as we attempt to disprove the best models.
As Tetlock says,

The single strongest predictor of rising into the ranks of superforecasters is perpetual beta, the degree to which one is committed to belief updating and self-improvement. It is roughly three times as powerful a predictor (of being a superforecaster) as its closest rival, intelligence. (p. 192)

Thus we will continuously challenge our results, combine results into ensembles (and ensembles of ensembles), with a goal of achieving the highest possible accuracy.
The combination of individual and ensembles of models, repeated with randomized data, provides much more accurate predictions and forecasts than models which do not use ensembles of models, nor randomize the data, as will be seen in many examples in this book. Over and over again, the ensemble models will beat the best published results, and usually by a large amount.
We will measure our results against a baseline (the basic linear model, which is always one of the models that will be used), keep a track record of those results, and find the patterns of the models that have the highest accuracy. All of this will be done in a way that is totally transparent and reproducible, as the examples in this book will show.

The biggest lesson for me in all of this work is how to make ensembles. You’ve already seen some of the steps, and there are more results to come. The second biggest lesson is that everything I was taught about how to do data science and AI was backwards to what actually works for me in real life. I’ve learned how I learn, and applied that skill (learning how I learn) to a wide range of skills, including:
• Running a multi-million dollar division of a Fortune 1000 company, including full profit and loss responsibility for several years.

The way that works for me is to start at the end, work backward from there, and never give up. Maybe the best evidence of the success of this method is this fact:
When I started to write the code that led to the Ensembles package, I followed those steps: Start at the end, work backward from there, and never give up. I wound up writing an average of 1,000 lines of clean, error free code per month for 15 months. The Ensembles package is around 15,000 lines of clean, error free code.
I found my attitude was much more important than my skill set, by a long shot.


3.14.6 How I stuck with it all the way to the end: The best career advice I ever received was from a homeless man I never met, and answers the question of what most strongly predicts success.



Ashford and Simpson


Learning about building ensembles will help you make more accurate predictions. That’s an extremely good skill to have in any setting. But I found the most important thing to predict is success. This has been studied, and there are quite a few good works on the subject, both academic and for the general population.
My favorite career advice—which I listened to nearly every day as I worked on the Ensembles project—is from a man who was homeless at the time he came up with the words.
Nick Ashford was from Willow Run, Michigan. He moved to New York city, hoping to get into the entertainment world as a dancer. Unfortunately he ended up homeless on the streets of New York. He slept on park benches, and got food from soup kitchens.
He heard that the people at White Rock Baptist Church would feed him (a homeless man) a normal meal, so Nick went there one Sunday morning. He met the people, especially the choir members, and started working with the piano player in the choir. Her name is Valerie Simpson.
Soon Nick and Valerie were writing songs for the church choir. Nick mentioned that while he was homeless, he realized that New York wasn’t going to “do me in”. He was determined. The words he put down say:
Ain’t no mountain high enough
Ain’t no valley long enough
Ain’t no river wide enough
Valerie took those words, and set them to music. They sent that song to Motown, who released it with Marvin Gaye and Tammy Terrell covering the vocals. It was later re-done by Ashford and Simpson and Paul Riser, with Diana Ross singing the lead.
As long as I am working on any project, I keep the words of Ashford and Simpson in mind. The very highest odds of success for everyone involved will be if we say there is no mountain high enough, no valley long enough or river wide enough to keep us from reaching our goal. I listened to those words nearly every day I was making the Ensembles package, and many days after while I was working on the Ensembles book that you are reading, and the website, https://www.ensembles1.com. Start from the end and work backwards. No matter what you are going through, the ending is absolutely worth the work that needs to be put in to get there, so just put the work in. In virtually all cases in my professional experience, the benefit has vastl outweighed the cost. Persisting until success has paid dividends far beyond anything I could have initially imagined.
While I have the skill of knowing how I learn (which I will continue to share with you in this book), this attitude of working no matter how high the mountain or long the valley or wide the river, gives me the how and the why to keep moving toward success, until that success is fully achieved, and the benefits go to everyone involved.

My journal was for crazy ideas, contradictory evidence, writing down my frustrations and successes, inspiration, the one next thing I worked on, and having a rock solid record of the path to success. Seeing the path I traversed was a huge motivation to finishing the project.
Do your best to add journal entries to your regular schedule.

Data Science Essay #1: How to Test What Is Most Important to your Customer (accuracy vs preparation) 
Many organizations believe their customer wants the most accurate models, and they work very hard to deliver those models to their customers. However, from a customer perspective, what they really want is to be prepared for anything that might come along. A very good data science solution will give the most accurate results, and also help the customer understand how these results can be used in a range of different perspectives.
Let’s use our results on the Boston Housing data set as a good starting point. While we can model the price within a certain degree of accuracy, customers virtually always appreciate the broader truth in the data. Let them know the margin of error (right now that is ±4.2, or ±$4,223), and anything else which will help them be better prepared for any changes that will come along.
We will achieve more accurate results in future chapters as we add more models and ensembles of models, but the best first step we can take is to be totally committed to the truth, as best we can report it, in a way that is as transparent as possible. We can also be committed to helping our customer be as well prepared as possible for changes which will happen, and show them how our models and help them be prepared for those changes.
While accuracy is a great result, it’s even better if your work also allows your customer to be as fully prepared as possible, given the data and the changes which impact all organizations.
The test to give your customer: The mean result is (insert mean result). However, there is a 16% chance the actual result will be above the mean result, and a 16% chance the actual result will be below the mean result. My professional recommendation is to have plans ready for each of the three situations, so you are ready for all possible results. Please let me know if there are any questions completing this, so you are best prepared, no matter what the result.
Please note that many organizations do not actually want the best results, what is most important to those organizations is maintaining the status quo. They will fight the best results like they are fighting an invading army, even when the evidence is overwhelming that the best results will vastly improve performance over current results and the team presenting the best results is on their side. Many will fight to protect the status quo at all costs, even at the expense of the best possible results. It is possible the most important outcome to your customer is keeping things as they are, not providing the best results. That will be true even if it means losing customers, market share, and staff. If their only path is to continue with the current results at all costs and against all options, the only solution I know is to walk away and work on something else. I have never had any success convincing any organization to pursue the best possible results if they are totally committed to the status quo at all costs and against all options.
This is a test.

6 Building weighted ensembles to model numerical data
In the last chapter we learned how to make 23 individual models, including calculating the error rate (as root mean squared error), and predictions from the holdout data (test and validation).
This chapter will show how to use those results to make weighted ensembles that can be used to model numerical data.
Let’s start at the end. Let’s imagine the finished product. A list of ensembles and individual models, with error rates sorted in decreasing order (best result on the top of the list)
Therefore we’re going to need a weighted ensemble. But what weight to use?
It turns out there is an excellent answer available for virtually no work on our part (which is great!). Each model has a mean error score. The weight we will use will be the reciprocal of the error.
Let’s say we have two models. One has an error rate of 5.0 and the other has an error rate of 2.0. Clearly the model with the error rate of 2.0 is superior to the model with the error rate of 5.0, since 2.0 is smaller than 5.0.
What we will do in building our ensemble is multiply the values in the ensemble by 1/(error rate). This will give higher weights to models with higher accuracy.
Let’s see how this works with an extremely simple ensemble.

library(MASS) # For the Boston Housing data set library(Metrics)
library(tidyverse)

  'tree' = tree_predictions / tree_RMSE_mean,

# Fit the tree model on the ensemble training data, predict on ensemble test data

)

results <- results %>% arrange(Error_Rate)

} # Closing brace for numresamples

6.1 Think before you do something. This will help when we start at the end and work backwards toward the beginning.
We are going to make an ensemble. The ensemble is going to a made of predictions from numerical models. You’ve already seen a couple of ensembles. This one will be extremely similar, but will involve more models.
Starting at the end, we want the error rate (root mean squared error) for the ensemble and prediction models.
That means we’ll need to make an ensemble. That means we’ll need individual model predictions, because that’s how an ensemble is made. If an ensemble is made of individual model predictions, that means we’ll need individual models. We already know how to do that, because we did it in the last chapter.
We’re going to build a simple ensemble with seven models, and then use that ensemble with four very different methods. The Ensembles package actually works with a total of 40 different models. The process is exactly the same, whether we are working with seven individual models or 23 individual models, five ensemble models or 17 ensemble models. The structre and methods are the same.
So let’s get started!
The seven individual models we will be building are:

Linear (tuned)
Bayesglm
Bayesrnn
Gradient Boosted
RandomForest
Trees

It’s important to understand that many other options are possible. Your are encouraged to add at least one more modeling method to the ensemble, and see how it impacts the results.
